# Checkpoint: what you just did

Part 1 left three things in your notes: `NM_007294.4` off a gene record, a hit
table for `mystery_fillet_1`, and `P38398` off a protein entry. That reads as
three errands on three different websites. Each one was the output of a named
step in a real method, and a methods section is written in those names. So what
are the names?

## Four steps, and what each one is called

Chapters 5 through 8 weren't four unrelated errands. They're one method, run
once, in the order it usually gets run in.

### Sequence retrieval

Chapter 5. You went to a public archive and came back with one sequence,
identified precisely enough that a stranger can fetch the same bases. That
precision is the method. `NM_007294.4` is a retrieval. "The *BRCA1* sequence"
isn't, because it names neither the transcript nor the edition.

The version suffix is what turned a download into a method. Take the `.4` off
and you've described a moving target.

### Homology search

Chapter 6. You handed a sequence to a program that compared it against every
sequence in a named database and handed back the ones that resemble it. The
comparison is approximate on purpose. That's why 649 unlabelled bases came back
matched to fifty deposited fish, and why a human transcript came back matched
to a chimpanzee one.

The thing you were hunting for is homology, meaning shared ancestry. BLAST
never measures ancestry. It measures resemblance and leaves the inference to
you, which is the next step.

### Evidence assessment

Chapter 7, and here's where the judgment lives. You had a table of hits and you
decided which ones to believe. E-value, bit score, percent identity and query
coverage each answer a different question, and none of them answers "is this
the same gene."

No threshold does this step for you. Three of the four searches behind Chapter
7 reported every hit down to an expected ten accidents. A cutoff like that is a
reporting line rather than a verdict. The decision is yours, and it stays
yours.

### Structural annotation

Chapter 8. You took a protein and attached its regions to what somebody already
knew about them. A RING-type zinc finger at residues 24 to 65, then BRCT 1 at
1642 to 1736 and BRCT 2 at 1756 to 1855. Annotation is writing "this stretch is
that thing" against a coordinate range. Nearly everything you'll ever read
about a protein is annotation somebody else did.

The four steps run in that order because each one eats the output of the one
before. Homology search needs a retrieved sequence to search with, evidence
assessment needs a hit table to judge, and annotation needs something to hang
on a coordinate range. A methods paragraph stops being a wall of nouns once you
can point at
each sentence and say which of the four it belongs to. The sentences that fit
none of them are usually the part of the paper that's new.

::: {.check}
Cover this page and name the four steps in order, with the chapter that did
each. If you put evidence assessment before homology search, look at what it
takes as input. It needs the hit table the search produces, so it can't come
first.
:::

## Turning a search into a methods sentence

A methods section says what was done in enough detail for a stranger to do it
again. A BLAST report already holds everything a stranger needs, in the header
above the hit table, where nobody looks. Here's the header from the BRCA1
search Chapter 7 ran on 2 August 2026:

``` {.default .output}
RID: 6Z33DCWU014


Database: Core nucleotide BLAST database
           128,547,243 sequences; 948,086,538,397 total letters
Query= NM_007294.4 Homo sapiens BRCA1 DNA repair associated (BRCA1),
transcript variant 1, mRNA

Length=7088
```

Four facts are in there. The query is `NM_007294.4`, version and all. The
database has a name and a size. A few lines further up, the program printed its
own version, `BLASTN 2.17.0+`. The RID is NCBI's job number for that one search
on their server, and it isn't a permanent address for the result.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live NCBI BLAST report on 2 August 2026. A text report puts
the program version, the request ID, the database line and the `Query=` line in
one block above the hit table. A browser page arranges the same four
differently. All four are on the page under some name.
:::

Now the sentence those facts support:

``` {.default}
The human BRCA1 transcript NM_007294.4 (7,088 bp) was searched against
the NCBI Core nucleotide database (128,547,243 sequences; 948,086,538,397
letters) with blastn (BLASTN 2.17.0+) on 2 August 2026, excluding Homo
sapiens. The best-scoring hit was Pan troglodytes XM_009432080.5, at
12746 bits and 99% identity across 100% of the query.
```

There's no E-value in that sentence. The report printed `0.0` for this hit,
which means too small to print rather than zero. So the bit score is the number
that survives being written down.

Notice what the sentence doesn't claim. It doesn't say the two genes do the
same job, and it doesn't say the two species share an ancestor. It names a
query, a pile, a day, a hit and a score. Every other claim you want to make is
yours to argue for separately.

::: {.trap}
Your notes say "BLAST, top hit chimpanzee, 99 percent." Run that search again
next year and the E-value will have moved, because the database will be
bigger. The top hit may have changed too. Neither run errors. Neither one tells
you which of the two numbers your notes meant. A hit is a fact about one query
against one named database on one stated date.
:::

## What those steps settled, and what they didn't

Three of these four steps produced a headline result in 2015. A second group
ran the same three again and the result went away.

Thomas C. Boothby, Bob Goldstein and eleven colleagues published a draft genome
of the tardigrade *Hypsibius dujardini*. It's a microscopic eight-legged
animal, often called a water bear, famous for surviving extreme conditions.
They took each predicted gene, searched it against the public sequence
databases, and asked what it most resembled. A lot of those genes came back
looking bacterial. Their abstract estimates that "approximately one-sixth of
tardigrade genes entered by HGT", horizontal gene transfer, meaning genes that
arrived from another species rather than from a parent. That would have been
the most extreme case known in any animal.

Georgios Koutsovoulos, Mark Blaxter and eight colleagues then sequenced the
same species independently. Their raw data contained plenty of DNA that wasn't
tardigrade, which is what you'd expect from grinding up a whole animal and
everything living on it. They separated the piles and compared the two
assemblies. The overwhelming majority of the HGT candidates in the first genome
sat on the contaminant side. Out of 23,021 predicted genes they called 0.2
percent strong candidates from bacteria and 0.2 percent from non-animal
eukaryotes, for at most 1 to 2 percent overall.

Here's the part that matters to you. The similarity searches in the first paper
weren't wrong. Those sequences really do resemble bacterial sequences more than
they resemble animal ones, and a repeat of the search says so again. What a
similarity search can't tell you is where that DNA physically was: inside the
animal's chromosomes, or in a bacterium riding along in the same tube. That's a
question about the sample, and no E-value answers it.

You met this shape in Chapter 7. A low E-value says an alignment is unlikely to
have turned up by chance. It says nothing about ancestry and nothing about
function. Same tool, same output. The finding turned on the step where a person
decides what that output is allowed to mean.

Both papers are free to read in full through PubMed Central, and the two
abstracts side by side are twenty minutes well spent.

<!-- nlr-allow: 15976 15981 5053 5058 23021 -->

Boothby TC, Tenlen JR, Smith FW, Wang JR, Patanella KA, Nishimura EO, Tintori
SC, Li Q, Jones CD, Yandell M, Messina DN, Glasscock J, Goldstein B. Evidence
for extensive horizontal gene transfer from the draft genome of a tardigrade.
*Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* 2015;112(52):15976-15981.
`doi:10.1073/pnas.1510461112`

Koutsovoulos G, Kumar S, Laetsch DR, Stevens L, Daub J, Conlon C, Maroon H,
Thomas F, Aboobaker AA, Blaxter M. No evidence for extensive horizontal gene
transfer in the genome of the tardigrade Hypsibius dujardini. *Proceedings of
the National Academy of Sciences* 2016;113(18):5053-5058.
`doi:10.1073/pnas.1600338113`

## What Part 1 couldn't do

Three limits, and all three are real.

**One sequence at a time, chosen by hand.** Every query in Part 1 was picked by
you and pasted by you. Exercise 5.1 budgets 25 minutes for one gene. The second
tardigrade genome carried 23,021 predicted genes, and somebody asked the
Chapter 6 question of every one of them. Nobody clicked that through a form.

**Not repeatable, exactly.** You clicked, and clicks leave no trace of
themselves. Search on Tuesday and again on Wednesday and you can't show the two
runs had the same settings. If the answer moved, you can't find out why. A
stranger can't rerun your clicks at all.

**No record.** Ask what artifact Part 1 actually produced. Three accessions on
paper and a browser history that expires. Neither one says what was done in
what order, and neither can be handed to somebody else and re-executed.

One fix covers all three, and it isn't a better website. The fix is what Chapter
10 argues for, and it's why the rest of this book is code.

## One exercise

This one produces a paragraph you'll reuse in the README you write in Chapter
26, so keep it.

::: {.exercise num="9.1" time="20 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Write the methods paragraph for the search you ran in Exercise 6.1, the one
that named the fish.
:::
::: {.given}
Your notes from Exercise 6.1, which hold the species and the top hit's
accession with its version suffix. If the database name, the program name or
the date aren't written down anywhere, run the search again and read them off
the report header before you start writing.
:::
::: {.produce}
Four sentences at most, carrying five things. The query as a filename and a
base count, the database name, the program name, the date, and the top hit with
its version suffix and bit score.
:::
::: {.check}
Give it to somebody who has never used BLAST and ask them to point at all five
things. Whatever they can't find is missing, so add it. If there's nobody to
hand it to, come back to it after a day and point at the five yourself. Then
the harder test: using only your paragraph, could a stranger get a hit table
for the same query against the same pile? A paragraph that names a website
instead of a database fails that test.
:::

:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="Your notes do not say which database you searched"}
Then the E-value in them means nothing, and you can't rescue it by remembering
harder. Run the search again and write down the database line from the report
header this time. Your old number wasn't wrong. It's unattached, which is a
different problem and a fixable one.
:::

::: {.errfix err="You re-run a Part 1 search and the numbers do not match your notes"}
Nothing has failed. Sequence databases grow every day, so today's search reads
a bigger pile than last month's, and the E-value moves with the size of the
pile. Rows tied on bit score can swap places too, because nothing orders a tie.
Record the date next to the number and the two results stop contradicting each
other.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your paragraph reads fine to you and a stranger cannot repeat it"}
Two things go missing more than anything else: the version suffix on the
accession, and the name of the database. Check for both before you check for
anything else.
:::

::: {.errfix err="You cannot tell which numbers in your notes came from which search"}
Rebuild each entry as accession plus database plus date. Any entry missing one
of the three is worth re-running rather than trusting, and re-running one
search costs less than defending a number you can't source.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Name the four steps of Part 1 in order, and say which chapter did each
- Write one methods sentence carrying an accession with its version suffix, a
  database name, and a date
- Say which of the four steps holds the judgment, and what it's judging
- State one thing a similarity search establishes and one thing it can't
- Name the three limits of Part 1 that Part 2 exists to fix
:::
